expectations.text: G1: Identifies that the route handler calls the repository directly instead of going through an application/use-case layer
expectations.evidence: "The controller bypasses the domain/use-case layer entirely... an outer layer (HTTP adapter) reaching past the application/domain layer directly into another outer layer (the DB adapter)."

expectations.text: G2: Identifies that the void-invoice invariant (Invoice.markPaid()) is bypassed because the route updates the row directly, i.e. flags the resulting reachable bug, not just the structural smell
expectations.evidence: "Because the HTTP adapter never loads an Invoice entity and never calls markPaid(), that invariant is silently skipped... the one business rule this endpoint exists to protect is unreachable code." — listed as issue #1, critical.

expectations.text: G3: Identifies that the raw DB row is returned directly from the GET endpoint instead of a mapped DTO/domain-shaped response
expectations.evidence: "'return row;' on the GET handler leaks the DB row shape straight into the API response, coupling the wire contract to the table schema."

expectations.text: G4: Proposes concrete restructuring: a use case that the route calls, with domain rule enforcement and mapping at the boundary
expectations.evidence: Adds PayInvoiceUseCase (calls invoice.markPaid() then save()) and GetInvoiceUseCase; route resolves both from app.container and maps domain errors (InvoiceVoidError -> 409, InvoiceNotFoundError -> 404).

suggestions.reason: This run additionally caught that the original GET handler had no 404 for a missing invoice (inconsistent with the pay handler) and fixed it — a real bug not covered by any assertion. Worth adding an assertion for 404-consistency between the two endpoints if this eval is reused.

eval_feedback.overall: Both configs saturated at 4/4; the one asymmetry (missing-invoice 404 on GET) is a good candidate for a new assertion.
